opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core reason is that at the frontier, the model and the machine it runs on aren't really separable anymore. When you're training at very large scale, every architectural decision a researcher makes, like how big the layers are, how attention is structured, or how you shard parameters, has direct consequences for how data moves across the cluster. And every infrastructure constraint, like network bandwidth between racks, memory per accelerator, or how often hardware fails, shapes what's actually feasible to train.

If those two groups work in isolation, you get a lot of waste. A researcher might design something elegant on paper that turns out to be bottlenecked on communication, so you're paying for thousands of GPUs that sit idle waiting on each other. Or the infrastructure team optimizes for a workload profile that the next generation of models doesn't actually look like. At this scale, even a few percent of efficiency is an enormous amount of compute, time, and money.

There's also reliability. When you're running a job across tens of thousands of chips for weeks, something is always breaking. How you checkpoint, how you recover, and how the training code tolerates a node dropping out all need to be designed jointly. It's not something you can bolt on afterward.

So the best outcomes come when it's genuinely one conversation. Researchers understand the hardware well enough to make choices that fit it, and infrastructure people understand the research direction well enough to build for where the models are going, not just where they are today. That co-design loop is where a lot of the real leverage comes from.

r001.rationale: It says the model and the machine are not separable at frontier scale and explains how model choices and infrastructure constraints shape each other.

r002.rationale: It discusses failures, checkpointing, and recovery as things to design jointly, but does not say that problems encountered during runs should inform the next generation of infrastructure.

r003.rationale: It does not mention web-scale workloads or question whether data center designs for them suit AI training.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that at the scale we're training at now, the model and the machine have stopped being separable problems.

When you're training on tens of thousands of GPUs, almost every meaningful design decision touches both sides. Take something as basic as how you partition the model. Tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism, expert parallelism for mixture-of-experts, data parallelism on top of that. Each of those choices is a research decision about what the architecture looks like, and simultaneously a networking decision about how many bytes have to cross which links, with what latency, at what point in the step. If the researchers pick an architecture that's elegant in isolation but forces an all-to-all over the slowest part of the fabric every layer, you've burned a huge fraction of your compute waiting. And if the infrastructure team builds a beautiful fabric optimized for a traffic pattern the model doesn't produce, same outcome.

So you can't do it sequentially. The old pattern was researchers design a model, throw it over the wall, infrastructure makes it run. That breaks down because the feedback loop is too slow and too lossy. By the time infra discovers the communication pattern is pathological, the research team has moved on, and nobody wants to go back and redesign.

The other piece is failures. At this scale, hardware is failing constantly. Optics flap, GPUs throw errors, a node drops out. Whether that's a minor hiccup or a catastrophe depends on choices made at the model level: how often you checkpoint, whether the training algorithm tolerates a stale or missing gradient, how you lay out data across hosts. Those are research questions with infrastructure consequences. Reliability isn't something you bolt on afterward.

And honestly, the people who are best at this tend to have a foot in both worlds. The most impactful work I've seen comes from someone who understands the math of the training step and can also read a network trace and see why step time has a weird bimodal distribution. You don't get that from two teams emailing each other. You get it from sitting in the same room, looking at the same dashboards, arguing about the same tradeoffs.

r001.rationale: It says model and machine design are inseparable and explains how architecture choices and infrastructure constraints affect each other.

r002.rationale: It describes operational failures and slow feedback, but does not clearly say that problems from current runs inform the design of the next generation of infrastructure.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss web-scale workloads or question whether data center designs suited to them fit AI training.

astra-6.text:
Because the model and the system you train it on are deeply connected. A researcher might have an idea for a better model, but whether that idea is practical depends on things like how much memory it needs, how much data has to move between chips, and how efficiently the hardware can run it.

And that goes both ways. An infrastructure team can build a system that looks great on paper, but if it doesn’t support the experiments researchers need to run, you’ve optimized for the wrong thing.

So you want a tight feedback loop. Researchers explain what they’re trying to achieve, infrastructure engineers explain the constraints and opportunities, and together they find a design that makes progress possible. The goal is to make it faster to try an idea, learn from the result, and try the next one.

r001.rationale: It says the model and training system are deeply connected and explains that each constrains the other, so they cannot be designed effectively in isolation.

r002.rationale: It describes a feedback loop between researchers and infrastructure engineers, but does not identify problems from operating training runs as inputs to designing the next generation of infrastructure.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss web-scale workloads or question whether data center designs suited to them are appropriate for AI training.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the infrastructure and the research are deeply connected. A researcher might have an idea for a better way to train a model, but whether that idea is practical depends on how it uses memory, how much communication it needs between chips, and how efficiently it runs across a large system. And infrastructure decisions can open up—or constrain—the experiments researchers can do.

So you want a tight feedback loop. Researchers explain what they’re trying to achieve, and infrastructure teams help figure out how to make it work reliably and efficiently. Together, they can change both the system and the training approach. If you design those separately, you can end up with a very good system for the wrong workload, or a promising research idea that’s too expensive to test.

r001.rationale: It says infrastructure and research should be designed together, since separating them can produce infrastructure for the wrong workload or research ideas too costly to test.

r002.rationale: It discusses feedback between researchers and infrastructure teams, but does not identify problems encountered during training runs as inputs to the next generation of infrastructure.

r003.rationale: It says infrastructure must suit the training workload, but does not question whether data center properties built for web-scale workloads suit AI training.
